tEn: Only Founders in the Building: Chris Pedregal & Euan Blair on Founder Problems
tZh: Only Founders in the Building：Chris Pedregal 与 Euan Blair 谈创始人的真实难题
sEn: Chris Pedregal and Euan Blair swap candid founder stories on inbox chaos, investor dynamics, and the hard conversations leaders must have.
sZh: Chris Pedregal 与 Euan Blair 坦诚分享创始人的真实困境：收件箱失控、投资人关系，以及领导者必须面对的艰难对话。

consensus.en: AI should augment humans, not replace them; human development remains primary.
consensus.zh: AI 应增强人类而非取代人类；人的发展始终是首要的。

consensus.en: Founders must be decisive and have strong opinions, especially on big things.
consensus.zh: 创始人必须果断，在大事上要有强烈观点。

consensus.en: Regular feedback and weekly one-on-ones are essential for developing people.
consensus.zh: 定期反馈和每周一对一沟通对人员发展至关重要。

consensus.en: The partner you choose in personal life is the most consequential career decision.
consensus.zh: 个人生活中选择的伴侣是最具影响力的职业决策。

consensus.en: Humans care about humans and relationships; this won't change with AI.
consensus.zh: 人类关心人类和人际关系；这不会因 AI 而改变。

consensus.en: Context and accountability are uniquely human strengths that AI struggles with.
consensus.zh: 上下文和问责是人类独有的优势，AI 难以企及。

contrarian.en: AI is best at coding, contrary to expectations that high-salary jobs are hardest to replace.
contrarian.zh: AI 最擅长编程，这与高薪工作最难被取代的预期相反。

contrarian.en: Don't outsource judgment to AI; engaging in judgment is uniquely human and essential.
contrarian.zh: 不要将判断外包给 AI；参与判断是人类独有且至关重要的。

contrarian.en: Universal basic income doesn't solve the loss of purpose from job displacement.
contrarian.zh: 全民基本收入无法解决工作被取代带来的目标感丧失。

contrarian.en: The naught-to-10 and 100-plus stages are harder than the middle scaling stage.
contrarian.zh: 从零到 1000 万和 1 亿以上的阶段比中间规模扩张阶段更难。

contrarian.en: Raising funding when you don't need it is key, as investor interest is inversely proportional.
contrarian.zh: 在不需要资金时融资是关键，因为投资者的兴趣与你需要的程度成反比。

contrarian.en: AI slop makes short, typo-ridden cold emails more effective than polished ones.
contrarian.zh: AI 生成的垃圾内容让简短、有错别字的冷邮件比精雕细琢的更有效。

turns.en: Welcome to Only Founders in the Building, a podcast from Founders Forum Group in collaboration with Audi, brought to you in partnership with Rothschild and Co. Some of the world's top entrepreneurs, CEOs, and innovators open up in one-to-one conversations with one another. No host, no interviewer, just two people crazy enough to pursue their own ideas, getting into what's really on our minds. Let's get started.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到 Only Founders in the Building，这是 Founders Forum Group 与 Audi 合作、并由 Rothschild and Co. 赞助的播客。一些世界顶级的企业家、CEO 和创新者在这里进行一对一的坦诚对话。没有主持人，没有采访者，只有两个疯狂到去追求自己想法的人，聊聊我们真正在想什么。我们开始吧。

turns.en: Delighted to be here with Chris, who has built the AI meeting notetaker of choice for anyone who loves their meetings getting transcribed effectively.
turns.zh: 很高兴和 Chris 在一起，他打造了 AI 会议记录工具，可以说是任何喜欢高效转录会议的人的首选。

turns.en: Thanks Yan. I'd like to introduce Yun, CEO and founder of Multiverse, the AI adoption layer for the workforce, which hopefully we can get into a little bit later because I think it's really interesting what that actually means. Looking forward to it.
turns.zh: 谢谢 Yan。我想介绍一下 Yun，Multiverse 的 CEO 兼创始人，为劳动力提供 AI 采用层，希望我们稍后能深入聊聊，因为我觉得这实际意味着什么非常有趣。很期待。

turns.en: So, first question for you. What's a founder problem that sounds ridiculous to everyone, but is actually kind of a real thing?
turns.zh: 那么，第一个问题问你。有什么创始人问题听起来很荒谬，但实际上却是个真问题？

turns.en: At one point, when Granola just started growing, my email inbox broke. I stopped being able to use email because I had so many emails coming in, cold emails, super important emails, completely mixed in, and there were just not enough hours in the day for me to do my job and also stay on top of my inbox. Which sounds really silly, but turns out you get an email from, I don't know, like a tax authority, and if you don't see that, it's a big deal. So there's some really important stuff that comes in there.
turns.zh: 有一次，Granola 刚开始增长的时候，我的收件箱爆了。我无法再使用电子邮件，因为涌入的邮件太多了，冷邮件、超级重要的邮件完全混在一起，而我一天根本没有足够的时间来完成工作并同时处理收件箱。这听起来很傻，但事实证明，你可能会收到来自税务局的邮件，如果你没看到，那就是大事。所以那里确实有一些非常重要的东西。

turns.en: What's happened to your inbox? You just stopped checking email.
turns.zh: 你的收件箱怎么了？你就停止查邮件了？

turns.en: I have an executive assistant who now filters it. But it's still tough though because it's hard for her to judge. She doesn't have context on everything.
turns.zh: 我现在有一位行政助理来过滤邮件。但仍然很难，因为她很难判断。她并不了解所有事情的背景。

turns.en: I can't bring myself to give over control of my inbox. So, what do you do? You read everything? Are you just better at email than me?
turns.zh: 我无法让自己放弃对收件箱的控制。那么，你怎么做？你读所有邮件？你只是比我更擅长处理邮件吗？

turns.en: Maybe I just get way fewer, Chris. The thing is, we're a B2B business and we're reaching out cold to businesses all the time. So, I always feel when someone reaches out cold, maybe I should at least give them the time of day if it's a well-written personalized email.
turns.zh: 也许我只是收到的邮件少得多，Chris。问题是，我们是一家 B2B 企业，我们一直在冷 outreach 联系企业。所以，我总是觉得当有人冷联系我时，如果是一封写得很好的个性化邮件，也许我至少应该给他们一点时间。

turns.en: That's the other thing. It's like there will be that diamond in the rough random person cold emails you, full of heart, and you immediately want to respond, but then there's just so much crap that goes in there as well.
turns.zh: 这是另一回事。就像会有那种沧海遗珠，一个随机的人冷邮件你，充满真心，你立刻就想回复，但那里也有太多垃圾。

turns.en: Well, and AI slop has made it worse. I found that I'm way more likely to respond to a short email with a typo in it rather than something that's like super thought out. It can be a much more human, much more real type of thing. Like not typo like careless typo like you can't as in if you can't spell a basic word. That's one kind of signal.
turns.zh: 嗯，AI 生成的垃圾让它更糟了。我发现我更可能回复一封有错字的简短邮件，而不是那种超级深思熟虑的东西。它可能是一种更人性、更真实的东西。不是那种粗心的错字，比如你连一个基本单词都拼不对。那是一种信号。

turns.en: Chris or Granola. Yeah. Yeah. What's another problem? I find that investors, how much investors want to talk to you is inversely proportional to how much you want to talk to them.
turns.zh: Chris 还是 Granola。是的。是的。另一个问题是什么？我发现投资者想和你交谈的程度与你想要和他们交谈的程度成反比。

turns.en: Yes. So, it's like whenever you want to talk to investors, it's really hard. And when you really don't want to talk to investors, if that ever happens, that's when they all want to talk to you. And then you're like, well, none of these people talked to me before, so I should probably talk to them now. But actually, I really don't need to talk to them now.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，就像每当你想要和投资者交谈时，那真的很难。而当你真的不想和投资者交谈时，如果那种情况发生，那就是他们都想和你交谈的时候。然后你会想，好吧，这些人以前都没和我谈过，所以我现在可能应该和他们谈谈。但实际上，我现在真的不需要和他们谈。

turns.en: It's why I always say raise funding when you don't need it. It's sort of like you gave me that advice, right? Because that's when they're talking to you.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么我总是说，在你不需要的时候融资。这有点像你给了我那个建议，对吧？因为那正是他们和你交谈的时候。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. God, the problem is though at a certain point there are only so many investors you're going to want to meet and have a good conversation with.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。天哪，但问题是，在某个时刻，你只想见那么多投资者并进行良好的对话。

turns.en: Yeah. Like it is. Yeah. You're right. It's a really That's a good Okay, good. Strong start.
turns.zh: 是的。就像它确实如此。是的。你说得对。这真的是一个很好的开始。

turns.en: Okay. Okay. Here we go. Yeah. I'm glad this is for you, not for me. What's a conversation you know you need to have but you haven't had yet?
turns.zh: 好的。好的。我们开始吧。是的。我很高兴这是给你的，不是给我的。有什么对话你知道你需要进行但还没有进行的？

turns.en: One of the things that you find on the startup journey is, and it's probably one of the big learnings I've had as you go through it, first, you learn to become a lot tougher than when you first started out, and you accept the fact that universal approval is not what you're after. You need to make a lot of tough decisions that often people will disagree with. And I think the hardest conversations are the ones where you have to give someone a combination of advice and feedback that you know will personally devastate them but will be really important for their development. And those are the hardest ones to do. They're the easiest ones to put off. Bad news never gets better with time. And the sooner you bring it to the table, the better. I have learned to actually have those conversations quite quickly because as you defer them, the compounding challenges of not giving someone the advice they really need to hear become harder, and it's actually kind of unfair on that person.
turns.zh: 在创业旅程中你会发现的一件事，也是我经历过程中最大的收获之一，首先，你学会了比刚开始时坚强得多，你接受了这样一个事实：普遍认可并不是你追求的目标。你需要做出很多艰难的决定，而人们常常会不同意。我认为最难的对话是那些你必须给某人建议和反馈的组合，你知道这会让他们个人崩溃，但对他们的发展至关重要。那些是最难做的。它们是最容易被推迟的。坏消息永远不会随着时间变好。你越早提出来越好。我已经学会了相当快地进行了这些对话，因为当你推迟它们时，不给予某人真正需要听到的建议所带来的复合挑战会变得更难，而且对那个人来说实际上有点不公平。

turns.en: Is there anything that helps you with those, like either a trigger to do it or how you do it?
turns.zh: 有什么能帮助你进行这些对话的吗，比如触发机制或你的做法？

turns.en: I think first, if you give feedback fairly regularly, it makes it easier because it's less jarring, and you're not waiting for a big six-monthly review. I think the other thing is if you have pretty trusted relationships with the people you work with, they understand where it's coming from. If they are suspicious of your motives or intent, it makes it a lot harder and it makes it hard for people to hear. So I think that's pretty important.
turns.zh: 我认为首先，如果你相当定期地给予反馈，这会更容易，因为不那么突兀，而且你不是在等待六个月一次的大考核。我认为另一件事是，如果你和你共事的人有相当信任的关系，他们理解你的出发点。如果他们怀疑你的动机或意图，那就难得多，也让人们难以听进去。所以我认为这很重要。

turns.en: Do you do like regular one-on-ones or?
turns.zh: 你会定期进行一对一吗，还是？

turns.en: Yeah, weekly one-on-ones. I think it's important.
turns.zh: 是的，每周一对一。我认为这很重要。

turns.en: And that's where you talk about this stuff.
turns.zh: 那就是你谈论这些事情的地方。

turns.en: Yeah, typically. I will say it's interesting. I spent a lot of the earlier part of the journey not really proactively having feedback conversations with people because I just didn't realize it was important. And the worst thing in any kind of manager relationship or even peer relationship at that moment is surprises. If someone's surprised by what you're telling them, then you probably messed up on your end.
turns.zh: 是的，通常如此。我会说这很有趣。在旅程的早期，我花了很长时间没有真正主动地与人们进行反馈对话，因为我只是没有意识到这很重要。在任何管理者关系甚至同事关系中，那一刻最糟糕的事情就是意外。如果某人对你告诉他们的内容感到惊讶，那么你那边可能搞砸了。

turns.en: Depending who you talk to, there's a big anti-one-on-one trend right now, at least with founders, where it's like if you give feedback, you should try to give feedback in front of other people so other people can learn from it as well. It takes a lot of time to do one-on-ones.
turns.zh: 取决于你和谁交谈，现在有一种强烈的反一对一趋势，至少在创始人中，就像如果你给反馈，你应该尝试在其他人面前给反馈，这样其他人也可以从中学习。做一对一会花费很多时间。

turns.en: I'm a big believer that AI in particular, but any technology should be augmenting humans and not replacing them. We are kind of the units of our people and their development is sort of primary.
turns.zh: 我坚信，尤其是 AI，任何技术都应该增强人类，而不是取代人类。我们某种程度上是以人为单位的，他们的发展是首要的。

turns.en: I think it's hard to develop people without one-on-ones. And the other big thing actually you learn on this journey that probably people don't talk about enough because there are a lot of kind of templates and specific founder styles that are put out there into the world is there is no one formula for doing it right.
turns.zh: 我认为没有一对一交流就很难发展人才。实际上，在这段旅程中你学到的另一件大事，可能人们谈论得不够多，因为世界上有很多模板和特定的创始人风格被传播，但并没有一个万能的公式能确保你做对。

turns.en: You've got to be you, you got to find the right combination between what's authentic to you and what's going to make your business successful. Like you can't sort of read a book on business or written by another founder and say I'm going to do this. I mean anyone who's listened to Jensen Huang talk about how he deals with his direct reports and management team.
turns.zh: 你必须做你自己，你必须在真实的你和让你的企业成功之间找到正确的组合。你不能读了一本商业书或另一位创始人写的书就说我要这么做。我的意思是，任何听过黄仁勋谈论他如何对待直接下属和管理团队的人都知道。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: That's an extreme example.
turns.zh: 那是个极端的例子。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的。是的。

turns.en: What's something about you that would surprise people who only know you as a founder? I like this one. It's quite deep.
turns.zh: 有什么关于你的事情会让只把你当作创始人的人感到惊讶？我喜欢这个问题。它挺深刻的。

turns.en: It is kind of deep. I guess like so Granola's grown recently, right? And at first there's just like five six of us in a room and we all knew each other really well. It was very casual.
turns.zh: 确实挺深刻的。我想想，Granola 最近发展壮大了，对吧？起初我们只有五六个人在一个房间里，我们彼此非常了解。非常随意。

turns.en: Now we're 70 80 people. So the new people who join like Chris is like that's Chris founder Chris, right? As opposed to just Chris. And I
turns.zh: 现在我们有七八十人。所以新加入的人会说 Chris 是那个创始人 Chris，对吧？而不是单纯的 Chris。而我

turns.en: I don't think I take myself very seriously. So, it's kind of weird when other people take that seriously. Um, so I it's like now when I walk into the office,
turns.zh: 我不觉得自己很严肃。所以当别人认真对待时，会有点奇怪。嗯，所以现在当我走进办公室，

turns.en: you know, I kind of I have to kind of like wear that.
turns.zh: 你知道，我有点不得不戴上那副面具。

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: You know, one way or another. Um,
turns.zh: 你知道，无论如何。嗯，

turns.en: and I think the thing that people don't necessarily realize is like when I walk into home that is gone. Like my kids do not care. My wife does not want to hear about granola anymore than she's heard before.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们不一定意识到的是，当我走进家门，那个身份就消失了。我的孩子们根本不在乎。我妻子不想再听到关于 Granola 的事了，她已经听够了。

turns.en: But it was funny. It's a guy from my team the other day was like we were talking about kids and they're like, "Oh, hey, Chris. Do you know who you're do you know do your kids know who you are?" And I was like, "Yeah, I'm Daddy and I'm the smelly guy who like, you know, can't sing and like can't dance well and like is like really silly."
turns.zh: 但很有趣。前几天我团队的一个家伙，我们在聊孩子，他说：“哦，嘿，Chris。你知道你的孩子知道你是谁吗？”我说：“知道啊，我是爸爸，我是那个臭臭的家伙，你知道，唱歌不好听，跳舞也不好，还特别傻。”

turns.en: And it's funny how you have to like it's almost like clothes you have to like take on and off. It's actually pretty important to take it off, I find. I think if you bring too much of that home, it's not good for anybody actually. But it's not always the easiest thing to take that stuff off.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这几乎就像衣服，你得穿上和脱下。我发现脱下来其实挺重要的。我觉得如果你把太多那种东西带回家，对谁都不好。但脱下来并不总是最容易的事。

turns.en: I think this is such a good one and like you know, we've talked before about being dads and kids and everything else cuz your kids kind of keep you grounded and down to earth. And you know, I saw this growing up with my dad, right? Going out there and doing a high-profile job. When he came home, we took the best out of him. Right. We made sure his feet stayed on the floor. And this is actually it's kind of important. It's one of the best things about having kids, having a partner who's going to tell you how it is, who knew you before, all of that kind of stuff and everything else because it is yeah, it's the most effective way of getting that real self.
turns.zh: 我觉得这个问题很好，你知道，我们之前谈过当爸爸、孩子等等，因为你的孩子会让你脚踏实地。你知道，我成长过程中看到我爸爸这样，对吧？出去做高调的工作。当他回家时，我们让他展现出最好的一面。我们确保他脚踏实地。这其实挺重要的。这是有孩子的好处之一，有一个会告诉你真相的伴侣，一个以前就认识你的人，所有这些东西，因为这是获得真实自我的最有效方式。

turns.en: But like this whole bring your whole self to work thing kind of every everyone's got to be a version of themselves at different times and different moments, right? Like it's just it's just life.
turns.zh: 但是像这种“把完整的自己带到工作中”的说法，每个人在不同时间不同时刻都必须是自己的一个版本，对吧？就像这就是生活。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

transcript.sec: Challenges and Growth as a Founder

turns.en: Where do you feel stretched beyond your expertise?
turns.zh: 你在哪里感到超出了你的专业领域？

turns.en: I mean, god, nearly everywhere, all of the time.
turns.zh: 我的天，几乎在所有地方，所有时候。

turns.en: Yeah, that's the nature of the job.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是工作的本质。

turns.en: It is. It's a, you know, in terms of things people don't probably talk about all that frequently. Like as a founder of a company, especially first-time founder, especially for many people kind of first time CEO, everything else, you are learning everything on the job and you start and you make a litany of mistakes and you're responsible initially for nearly everything that happens in the business.
turns.zh: 是的。你知道，就人们可能不常谈论的事情而言。作为公司的创始人，尤其是首次创始人，尤其对很多人来说是首次 CEO 等等，你在工作中学习一切，你开始时会犯一连串错误，最初你几乎对业务中发生的一切负责。

turns.en: Then your kind of purview becomes narrower and narrower, but you still got to hold to account amazing domain specialists who have infinitely more experience in their field than you do. And yet you're still their boss and you have to coax the best out of them and challenge them on the right things and everything else.
turns.zh: 然后你的视野变得越来越窄，但你仍然要管理那些在你领域比你经验丰富得多的优秀专家。然而你仍然是他们的老板，你必须引导他们发挥出最好的水平，在正确的事情上挑战他们等等。

turns.en: So I think the job is basically kind of an inherent stretch all the way through and the thing you have to get comfortable with is that that's kind of okay because almost every other founder, every other CEO is the same. It's you know there are ways you can bolster it, right? Get coaching, get great board members, get people around you who can tell you when you're kind of,
turns.zh: 所以我认为这份工作基本上从头到尾都是一种内在的拉伸，你必须习惯的是这没什么，因为几乎其他所有创始人、所有 CEO 都是这样。你知道有办法可以加强，对吧？找教练，找优秀的董事会成员，让周围的人在你有点……的时候告诉你，

turns.en: you know, being a complete idiot and whatever else because it's not always easy for your team to tell you that.
turns.zh: 你知道，当你完全是个白痴或其他什么的时候，因为你的团队并不总是容易告诉你这些。

turns.en: Um, and I think it's the nature of the journey. The other thing that changes so much is what's required of you is dramatically different from the naught to 10 million stage, the 10 to 100 million stage, and the 100 million plus stage. I actually think the naught to 10 and the 100 plus are so much harder than the bit in the middle because once you got product market fit and the organization's kind of up and running and you've got some structure in place, you can really go and it gets a little easier for a while and then you enter this new realm again.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为这是旅程的本质。另一件变化很大的事情是，对你的要求从零到 1000 万美元阶段、1000 万到 1 亿美元阶段、1 亿美元以上阶段截然不同。我实际上认为从零到 1000 万和 1 亿以上比中间部分难得多，因为一旦你找到了产品市场契合点，组织开始运转，你有了一些结构，你就可以真正前进，会变得容易一些，然后你又进入一个新的领域。

turns.en: And what happens at 100 plus asking
turns.zh: 那么在 1 亿以上会发生什么？

turns.en: basically yeah you've basically got to the trick that kind of got you there you've got to evolve beyond and you've got to figure out like what does the next incarnation of this company look like if you want to go public one day what does a public markets ready version of the company look like the naught to 100 there's enough in most businesses that get venture capital there's enough there for the initial idea to scale 100 million it's when you get beyond that I think it it it becomes you know, you've got to figure out how to reinvent yourself on the job, both as a leader, but also the company itself.
turns.zh: 基本上，是的，你基本上已经掌握了让你达到那里的技巧，你必须超越它，你必须弄清楚，如果你有朝一日想上市，公司的下一个化身会是什么样子，一个准备好进入公开市场的公司版本会是什么样子。从零到 1 亿，大多数获得风险投资的企业都有足够的空间让最初的想法扩展到 1 亿，但当你超越那个阶段，我认为就变成了，你知道，你必须弄清楚如何在工作中重塑自己，既是作为领导者，也是公司本身。

turns.en: Here's a question. It sounds like you don't necessarily have a lot of control. There's the biggest issue or fire or thing that business needs to do and you need to get good at that. And sometimes those things you might enjoy and might be fun for you and sometimes you probably don't enjoy it. Like I don't know how much you care about public markets or becoming, you know, any advice on that?
turns.zh: 这里有个问题。听起来你不一定有太多控制权。总有最大的问题或火或业务需要做的事情，你需要擅长它。有时那些事情你可能喜欢，可能有趣，有时你可能不喜欢。比如我不知道你有多关心公开市场或成为，你知道，有什么建议吗？

turns.en: It's a great question. I think and I can think a number of bits of the job that I don't naturally gravitate towards.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。我想我能想到一些我不自然倾向的工作部分。

turns.en: I think those are where, as you build out a kind of CEO office, chief of staff, other things like people who can basically cover for some of your weaknesses or deficiencies, or just things you don't want to spend time on, are really important. I also think, though, you have to learn to be able to keep your eye in and get sufficiently good at those things that it doesn't become debilitating to the business. Because in the end, there's a lot of talk about founder mode and CEOs sort of needing to be more prominent and play driving roles in their companies more than ever because of how fast the market's moving. It does mean you can't just be a specialist. You've got to still remain a reasonably accomplished generalist, and that requires speaking to people, understanding what's happening in the world. Also, things like this founders forum — you've got to be plugged in. You've got to speak to people, and it's almost like a weird form of founder therapy, speaking to other founders.
turns.zh: 我觉得这些地方正是——当你搭建起类似 CEO 办公室、幕僚长这样的角色，也就是能基本补上你某些弱点或短板、或者只是你不想花时间处理的事情的人——这些人非常重要。但我也认为，你得学会保持手感，在这些事情上做到足够好，不至于拖累整个业务。因为归根结底，现在有很多关于创始人模式的讨论，说 CEO 需要比以前更突出、在公司里扮演更强的驱动角色，因为市场变化太快了。这确实意味着你不能只做一个专才。你还得保持自己是一个相当有造诣的通才，而这需要你去和人交流、去理解世界上正在发生什么。还有像这个创始人论坛——你得参与进去，得和人交流，这几乎像是一种奇怪的创始人心理治疗，和其他创始人聊聊。

turns.en: And it's amazing how analogous the problem sets are from company to company. Everyone's basically dealing with a similar version of the same problem most of the time.
turns.zh: 而且令人惊讶的是，各家公司的难题集竟然如此相似。大多数时候，每个人基本上都在处理同一个问题的相似版本。

turns.en: And how do you cover for your gaps, or do you not have any gaps?
turns.zh: 那你怎么补上自己的短板，还是说你根本没有短板？

turns.en: I have tons of gaps. I have tons of gaps. I find that — maybe one thing is that, for me, I love product. That's what gives me energy. And I've realized that if I don't make sure I have some of the stuff that gives me joy or energy, then I have less energy for everything else. And in a somewhat counterintuitive way, it's almost like I can be more productive at the stuff I'm not as good at or don't enjoy if I get to do some of the stuff that I love, because it just kind of reminds me — it's not even a conscious thing. It just actively gives me joy, and other things are just very energy draining. And as the founder, we have to deal with whatever is most important for the company at any given time.
turns.zh: 我有一大堆短板。我有一大堆短板。我发现——也许有一点是，对我来说，我热爱产品，那是给我能量的事。我意识到，如果我不确保自己做一些能带给我快乐或能量的事，那我对其他所有事情的精力都会更少。而且有点反直觉的是，如果我能做一些我热爱的事，我反而能在那些我不擅长或不喜欢的事情上更高效，因为它会提醒我——这甚至不是有意识的事。它就是主动给我快乐，而其他事情就是非常消耗精力。而作为创始人，我们必须处理公司当下最重要的事情。

turns.en: And that definitely changes.
turns.zh: 而这肯定会变。

turns.en: And that changes all the time, right? And it's usually something — at least for us, for me — that I'm not great at, because it's either something we've never dealt with before or something that's gone sideways. But I've also found that managing my state — my energy, my mood, my morale, my headspace — is actually a really important function.
turns.zh: 而且它一直在变，对吧？而且通常都是——至少对我们、对我来说——我不太擅长的事，因为它要么是我们从未处理过的事，要么是出了岔子的事。但我也发现，管理自己的状态——我的能量、情绪、士气、心态——其实是一项非常重要的职能。

turns.en: Does a founder need a following?
turns.zh: 创始人需要追随者吗？

turns.en: There's a lot to unpack in there.
turns.zh: 这里面有很多可以展开的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: I guess starting something and making it a thing in the world is hard, and it's likely not going to work. So you're kind of fighting against the odds. So you kind of have to do whatever is necessary to make that work. I personally hate Twitter or X.
turns.zh: 我想，开始做一件事并让它在这个世界上成为现实是很难的，而且很可能不会成功。所以你是在逆势而为。所以你不得不做任何必要的事让它成功。我个人讨厌 Twitter 或者说 X。

turns.en: Are you on it?
turns.zh: 你在上面吗？

turns.en: I'm on it. I'm on it for Granola.
turns.zh: 我在上面。我是为了 Granola 才在上面。

turns.en: You're what?
turns.zh: 你什么？

turns.en: Okay. I'm not on it.
turns.zh: 好吧。我不在上面。

turns.en: You're not on it? Were you ever on it?
turns.zh: 你不在上面？你以前在上面过吗？

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.en: No. Do you think it ever would have benefited Multiverse for you to be on it?
turns.zh: 没有。你觉得如果你在上面，会对 Multiverse 有帮助吗？

turns.en: I was told at various times that it might, but I couldn't bring myself to do it.
turns.zh: 不同时期有人告诉我可能会有帮助，但我就是做不到。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, so I hate it. Yet a lot of Granola's early growth came from folks posting on Twitter. And that was the hardest, because we didn't really have a growth plan. We just put the product out. And luckily some people retweeted my tweet. I had, I think, zero following basically, but some folks retweeted it and it got some attention and kind of grew from there. But I have such a — it's mostly not a love-hate. It's like, oh, I understand the value and there's some great things that have come out of this, but I also kind of hate what this does to my headspace. Also being in London is tough because I want to post basically when people wake up. So I'm always tweeting, but if we have a new feature launch, I'll post at like 5 p.m. And then I can't help but want to see the comments or the messages I'm getting. And then it's like 8, it's like bedtime with the kids and I'm looking at it and I'm like, oh, there's some jerk on the internet, or like now I'm worried about what that jerk is saying.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，我讨厌它。然而 Granola 早期的很多增长来自人们在 Twitter 上发帖。那是最难的，因为我们其实没有增长计划。我们只是把产品放出去。幸运的是有些人转发了我的推文。我当时基本上零粉丝，但有些人转发了它，它获得了一些关注，然后就从那里增长起来。但我有这样一种——它主要不是爱恨交加。而是像，哦，我理解它的价值，它带来了一些很棒的东西，但我也讨厌它对我的心态造成的影响。另外在伦敦也很麻烦，因为我想在人们醒来的时候发帖。所以我总是在发推，但如果我们发布新功能，我会在下午 5 点左右发。然后我就忍不住想去看评论或收到的消息。然后到了 8 点，到了孩子睡觉的时间，我还在看，我就想，哦，网上有个混蛋，或者现在我开始担心那个混蛋在说什么。

turns.en: But LinkedIn is a much kind of — I don't even — that's interesting. I don't go on LinkedIn. My COO reads it for fun, which breaks my brain, honestly. But good on your COO.
turns.zh: 但 LinkedIn 是一种更——我甚至——那很有意思。我不上 LinkedIn。我的 COO 把它当消遣读，说实话这让我脑子转不过来。但你的 COO 真不错。

turns.en: I guess the one thing about it is, clearly everyone has — if you look at Twitter, especially tech Twitter, AI Twitter, that's where a lot of the conversation's happening. And everyone has these vested interests, and you can take it to be more transactional or less transactional, but it doesn't come to me naturally. It definitely takes a lot of energy for me to do it. So I don't post very much.
turns.zh: 我想关于它的一点是，显然每个人都有——如果你看 Twitter，尤其是科技圈 Twitter、AI 圈 Twitter，很多对话都在那里发生。每个人都有这些既得利益，你可以把它看得更交易性或者不那么交易性，但它对我来说不自然。做这件事确实要花我很多精力。所以我发得不多。

turns.en: Does your team try and cajole you to do it more?
turns.zh: 你的团队会试着哄你多发一些吗？

turns.en: So we tried to hire a team — there's these consulting firms that'll write content for you.
turns.zh: 我们试过雇一个团队——有一些咨询公司会帮你写内容。

turns.en: Complete crap.
turns.zh: 完全是垃圾。

turns.en: Yeah, of course. Complete. It's not their fault, but it's just kind of like — and it probably would have worked in a sense. Probably would have gotten impressions, but that was too much for me. Something about you don't want to put out an inauthentic version of yourself or your thoughts or whatever else in there, because in the end we kind of care about being who we are, right? I think that's important.
turns.zh: 是啊，当然。完全是。这不是他们的错，但就是有点像——从某种意义上说它可能也会有效。可能会获得曝光，但对我来说太过头了。关于你不想在那里放出一个不真实的自己、你的想法或其他什么，因为归根结底我们在乎的是做自己，对吧？我觉得那很重要。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think you can't really outsource that.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，我觉得那东西没法外包。

turns.en: Exactly. It's — before you were talking about expertise, and the thing that was going through my mind is, there's all these areas where you don't have expertise. The one thing you are an expert in is you're an expert in being you, and in a weird way that's actually extremely important for the company, right? And it's not because you're brilliant or right or wrong. It's just because the company needs to have an identity and a direction — founder company — and that's the founder, right? And that was a bit uncomfortable for me in the early days. But now I've realized —
turns.zh: 正是。这——你之前谈到专业能力，我脑子里想的是，有那么多领域你并不专业。你唯一专业的事情就是做你自己，而奇怪的是，这对公司其实极其重要，对吧？这不是因为你才华横溢或对或错。只是因为公司需要有一个身份和一个方向——创始人公司——而那就是创始人，对吧？早期这让我有点不舒服。但现在我意识到——

turns.en: So you learned to embrace it.
turns.zh: 所以你学会了拥抱它。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I've learned to embrace it.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我学会了拥抱它。

turns.en: Was there a moment or a bit of advice or anything else where you...
turns.zh: 有没有那么一个时刻，或者一点建议，或者别的什么，让你……

turns.en: I always struggle a little—I like building product—and something I've always struggled with as a leader is that, in a weird way, this is a power dynamic that's never been very comfortable for me. If we could just be flat and collaborate on stuff, I would naturally gravitate towards that. It became clear to me when folks on my team were like, 'No, no, I just need to know the way we do this.' And someone took me aside—I can't remember who right now—and said, 'It actually doesn't matter what you choose. We just need to choose something and it needs to be consistent with all the other things we do.' If you go into our office, it doesn't feel very corporate. It's a bunch of furniture we bought secondhand at vintage stores.
turns.zh: 我总是有点纠结——我喜欢做产品——而作为领导者，我一直不太适应这种权力动态，说来奇怪，这让我一直不太舒服。如果我们能扁平化、一起协作，我会自然而然地倾向于那样。当团队里的人对我说‘不，不，我只需要知道我们怎么做这件事’时，我才明白过来。有人把我拉到一边——我一时想不起是谁——说：‘其实你选什么并不重要。我们只需要选定一个，并且要和我们做的其他所有事情保持一致。’如果你走进我们的办公室，它感觉不太像公司。里面全是我们从二手店淘来的家具。

turns.en: Which is random—like there's no... that's not good or bad, but it's like...
turns.zh: 这很随意——就像没有……这没有好坏之分，但就像……

turns.en: It wasn't some big statement about the company.
turns.zh: 这并不是关于公司的什么大声明。

turns.en: Correct, but it is kind of consistent with how the product feels, you know what I mean? It doesn't feel very corporate, and that's actually important. There's a thread that connects those.
turns.zh: 没错，但这和产品的感觉是一致的，你明白我的意思吗？它感觉不太像公司，这其实很重要。有一条线把这些连接起来。

turns.en: And in a weird way, the thread that connects those is Sam and I—my co-founder and I. So I've become more comfortable with that rule.
turns.zh: 说来奇怪，连接这些的线就是 Sam 和我——我的联合创始人和我。所以我对这条规则越来越适应了。

turns.en: To that point, you have a pretty profound responsibility as a founder in particular, but I think probably most CEOs, most leaders, to be decisive, right? You have to have a strong opinion, and it doesn't mean that opinion always wins out or whatever else, but most of the time people expect you to have a view of the way things should be or the way they should be done. And so the point before in following, it's much easier—whether you agree or disagree with someone—it's easier to follow them if they have a pretty strong sense of belief. And that is really important because there's never an expectation to get the decision right all the time. We've all made plenty of mistakes on this journey. It's how you learn. But I do think you can't abrogate yourself of the responsibility of needing to have a strong opinion, certainly on the things that matter. It can get exhausting if you have a strong opinion on absolutely everything, but the big things—it's kind of a requirement.
turns.zh: 说到这一点，尤其是作为创始人，但我认为大多数 CEO、大多数领导者，都有相当重大的责任去果断决策，对吧？你必须有一个强烈的观点，这并不意味着那个观点总是赢，或者别的什么，但大多数时候人们期望你对事情应该怎样或应该怎么做有自己的看法。所以之前关于跟随的观点，无论你同意还是不同意某人，如果他们有一个相当强烈的信念，跟随他们会容易得多。这真的很重要，因为从来没有人期望你总是做出正确的决定。我们在这段旅程中都犯过很多错误。这就是你学习的方式。但我确实认为，你不能免除自己需要有一个强烈观点的责任，尤其是在重要的事情上。如果你对绝对所有事情都有强烈观点，那会让人筋疲力尽，但大事上——这算是一种要求。

turns.en: Okay. So this question is from Rothschild. What advice do you find yourself giving repeatedly?
turns.zh: 好的。所以这个问题来自 Rothschild。你发现自己反复给出的建议是什么？

turns.en: Okay. I say a couple of things quite a lot that are more about personal life or personal life decisions. One of them is—and I was given this advice and it's definitely turned out to be true—the person you end up partnering up with in your personal life, wife, husband, whatever, is probably the single most consequential decision you'll make for the arc of your career and how successful you can be.
turns.zh: 好的。我经常说几件事，更多是关于个人生活或个人生活决策的。其中之一是——我得到过这个建议，而且它确实被证明是真的——你在个人生活中最终结伴的人，妻子、丈夫， whatever，可能是你为职业生涯的轨迹以及你能有多成功所做的最重要的决定。

turns.en: Right? It is the arc of your life or arc of your career.
turns.zh: 对吧？这是你人生的轨迹或职业生涯的轨迹。

turns.en: Arc. So life, I think most people get that—that's fairly clear. But career, people underestimate that. Someone who can challenge you, make you better, support you when that's needed—it's so critical and a lot of people don't think that. I meet plenty of single founders and often when they ask me, 'Hey, what should I say?'—find someone. These journeys are horrific if you're having to do them alone. And the other thing I say a lot to people is have kids. Not just because we probably could do with people having a few more children, but because in terms of your ability to prioritize, put stuff in perspective, and have an outlet that isn't—the founder journey becomes all-consuming work—and just something that is nothing to do with that. You talked before about how you're a different person at home versus when you're in work. And one of the hardest things to do as a founder, CEO, responsible for so many things, is just be a ruthless prioritizer, and kids kind of force you to engage with that whether you want to or not because—
turns.zh: 轨迹。所以人生，我想大多数人都明白——那相当清楚。但职业，人们低估了这一点。一个能挑战你、让你变得更好、在需要时支持你的人——这太关键了，而很多人不这么想。我遇到过很多单身创始人，当他们问我‘嘿，我该怎么办？’——找个人。如果你不得不独自走这些旅程，那太可怕了。我经常对人们说的另一件事是生孩子。不仅仅是因为我们可能确实需要人们多生几个孩子，而是因为就你优先排序的能力、把事情看透、以及有一个不是——创始人旅程会变成吞噬一切的工作——的出口，而且和那完全无关。你之前谈到过你在家和在工作时是不同的人。作为创始人、CEO，负责这么多事情，最难的事情之一就是做一个无情的优先排序者，而孩子会强迫你面对这一点，不管你想不想，因为——

turns.en: Yeah. They're non-negotiable.
turns.zh: 是的。他们没得商量。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Like you can stop going to the gym, you can stop seeing your friends. Like I guess you can stop seeing your kids a little bit, but that doesn't last very long.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的。就像你可以停止去健身房，你可以停止见朋友。我想你可以稍微停止见孩子，但那持续不了多久。

turns.en: Yeah. Never considered that option.
turns.zh: 是的。从没考虑过那个选项。

turns.en: What human quality will technology most struggle to replicate? Chris, it's a pretty live conversation.
turns.zh: 技术最难复制的人类品质是什么？Chris，这是一个相当热门的话题。

turns.en: I mean it's a really interesting question, right? On Twitter, people love to shout about this all the time. I think people are very surprised by—for example, AI is best at coding right now, right? And I don't think that's what people expected. That's definitely not what I expected because that's a very high-paid job that people are highly educated, lots of training, and all of a sudden computers can kind of come in and—
turns.zh: 我是说，这确实是个有趣的问题，对吧？在 Twitter 上，人们总是喜欢大声讨论这个。我觉得人们非常惊讶——例如，AI 现在最擅长编程，对吧？我不认为这是人们预期的。这绝对不是我所预期的，因为那是一份高薪工作，人们受过高等教育，大量培训，突然之间计算机就能进来——

turns.en: Yeah. The hierarchy has always been almost always the bigger your salary presumably the harder it is to replace.
turns.zh: 是的。等级制度几乎总是——你的薪水越高， presumably 就越难被取代。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Exactly. So I don't think anything is off limits. I think computers are going to get really good at almost all those things. To me, the point is though—and I'm curious what you think about this—humans care about humans. We don't care about machines. We care about people and we care about relationships. And we're naturally wired that way. And that's not going to change, right? And so it's like computers are going to replicate everything. I think AI is going to get really good at generating almost anything, right? And ultimately what we're still going to want the same things and we're still going to want to relate to people in the same ways. So I don't think it really matters—maybe my point here. There might be some—I don't know—I think maybe a plumber might be the one that gets—the hardest to replicate because it's a bunch of—or there's some types of jobs that are a mix of manual and very different from one problem to the next and yada yada yada. But I think this idea of oh there's some corner of tasks or intelligence that'll all be saved—I don't believe in that, but I don't think it matters is the short of it. What's your take?
turns.zh: 是的。是的。没错。所以我不认为有什么是禁区。我认为计算机将在几乎所有那些事情上变得非常擅长。对我来说，关键是——我很好奇你怎么看——人类关心人类。我们不关心机器。我们关心人，我们关心关系。我们天生就是这样。这不会改变，对吧？所以就像计算机将复制一切。我认为 AI 将非常擅长生成几乎任何东西，对吧？最终我们仍然会想要同样的东西，我们仍然会以同样的方式与人建立关系。所以我不认为这真的重要——也许这是我的观点。可能有一些——我不知道——我认为也许水管工可能是最难复制的，因为那是一堆——或者有些类型的工作是体力劳动和非常不同的问题的混合，等等等等。但我认为这种想法——哦，有些任务或智能的角落会被保留下来——我不相信这一点，但我不认为这重要，简而言之。你怎么看？

turns.en: I largely agree.
turns.zh: 我大体上同意。

turns.en: I think if you look at the moment, one of the things that is both really necessary because AI is not good at it, but also quite defensible for humans is context, right? And I see that.
turns.zh: 我认为如果你看看当下，有一件事既非常必要——因为 AI 不擅长它——又对人类来说相当有防御性，那就是上下文，对吧？我看到了这一点。

turns.en: What do you mean by that?
turns.zh: 你这是什么意思？

turns.en: So if you look at the work we do training people on the job, we work a lot with frontline workers because they have so much context around how their job needs to be done and what to look out for in any given situation. They have that pattern recognition. They have that contextual layer they've built on the job. And AI, while it might be commoditizing expertise, struggles with that kind of context gap. And so training humans to embrace AI and turn their context into expertise and turbocharge them is really beneficial. We're finding that accountability is another good one. There's a reason we continue to have human coaches, quite apart from the fact that people love working with other humans, but you can hold someone accountable to turn up for a meeting with them. If an agent asks you to show up at a certain time, it might not be the top of your priority list.
turns.zh: 所以如果你看看我们在工作中培训人们的工作，我们经常与一线员工合作，因为他们对于如何完成工作以及在任何特定情况下要注意什么有着丰富的上下文。他们有那种模式识别能力。他们在工作中建立了那种上下文层次。而 AI，虽然它可能正在使专业知识商品化，但在这种上下文差距上却举步维艰。因此，培训人们拥抱 AI，将他们的上下文转化为专业知识并增强他们的能力，是非常有益的。我们发现问责制是另一个好的方面。我们继续拥有人类教练是有原因的，除了人们喜欢与其他人合作之外，你可以让某人对与你见面负责。如果一个智能体要求你在某个时间出现，那可能不是你的首要任务。

turns.en: Disappoint organizations based on especially more experienced people and people in leadership positions based on their judgment and the one thing I really hate is when people outsource judgment to AI, right? For lots of reasons, you know, ethical, philosophical, everything else, but it's one of the few things we have that is pretty uniquely human at the moment. And chucking something, you know, a document that they're supposed to review into a model, asking it to give them thoughts and opinions and then sharing those verbatim. You got to engage in judgment.
turns.zh: 让组织失望，尤其是更有经验的人和领导职位的人，基于他们的判断，而我真的讨厌的一件事是人们将判断外包给 AI，对吧？出于很多原因，你知道，伦理、哲学等等，但这是我们目前拥有的少数相当独特的人类特质之一。把一些东西，比如他们应该审查的文件扔进模型，要求它给出想法和意见，然后逐字分享。你必须参与判断。

turns.en: Judgment is interesting because two very important things for judgment are values and then accountability, right? So I agree with you on the accountability. It's like, okay, you don't want to—we're not wired to care about letting down an AI, but if you let down a human, you show up five, ten minutes late to a meeting with a human, you're a bit sheepish.
turns.zh: 判断很有趣，因为判断的两个非常重要的东西是价值观和问责制，对吧？所以我同意你关于问责制的观点。就像，好吧，你不想——我们天生不会关心让 AI 失望，但如果你让一个人失望，你与一个人开会迟到五到十分钟，你会有点不好意思。

turns.en: Yeah. You're going to feel bad about that. It's also the other way around where you want someone to be responsible. Like if we make the wrong call and something bad happens, you want a human to own that, right? Because you can't have an agent own that, right? And the accountability is a really good point on accountability.
turns.zh: 是的。你会为此感到难过。反过来也是如此，你希望有人负责。就像如果我们做出错误的决定，发生了不好的事情，你希望一个人来承担，对吧？因为你不能让一个智能体承担，对吧？而问责制——关于问责制，这是一个非常好的观点。

turns.en: It goes both ways. Yeah. And then judgment again—a lot of who you choose to work with comes down to judgment. And I think judgment comes down to in large part values. Like there's lots of people who make different decisions in the same situation. How do you elect your team or what your company—like how do you think about problems or what trade-offs do you choose to make? Though I think AI is going to change everything and kind of nothing—not nothing but it's going to change everything in terms of how we work but I think the lived experience that people are going to have is not going to change all that much. That's kind of where I'm settling, or maybe choosing to settle, and the arc of technology so far kind of has more or less been born out that way. There is a debate as to whether this is just so uniquely different from anything that's come before it. But again, humans are pretty terrible when it comes to trying to predict the future on these things. So, we just don't know.
turns.zh: 这是双向的。是的。然后判断 again——你选择与谁合作很大程度上归结为判断。而我认为判断很大程度上归结为价值观。就像有很多人在相同情况下做出不同的决定。你如何选择你的团队或你的公司——比如你如何思考问题，或者你选择做出什么权衡？尽管我认为 AI 将改变一切，又几乎什么都不改变——不是什么都不改变，而是它将在我们的工作方式上改变一切，但我认为人们将拥有的生活体验不会有太大变化。这就是我逐渐安顿下来的地方，或者可能是选择安顿下来，而迄今为止技术的弧线或多或少已经证明了这一点。有一个争论是，这是否与之前任何事物都如此独特地不同。但再次强调，人类在预测这些事情上的未来方面相当糟糕。所以，我们就是不知道。

turns.en: I think the other thing is however capable AI gets, don't underestimate the fact that governments will still be creating the rules, right? At least in the near term, and there'll probably be demands from their populations to really make sure they're enforcing those rules. Companies will continue to create the rules and be restricted—data privacy, legal, information security, everything else—that there will be this divergence between what the models are capable of and what we're actually permitting. And some of the most interesting debates humanity is going to have will be where do we draw those lines and what do we sacrifice in order to reach some of those promised gains.
turns.zh: 我认为另一件事是，无论 AI 变得多么有能力，不要低估政府仍将制定规则这一事实，对吧？至少在短期内，而且可能会有来自民众的要求，真正确保他们执行这些规则。公司将继续制定规则并受到限制——数据隐私、法律、信息安全等等——模型的能力与我们实际允许的范围之间将存在分歧。而人类将进行的一些最有趣的辩论将是：我们在哪里划清界限，以及为了达到一些承诺的收益，我们牺牲什么。

turns.en: And over what time horizon as well, right? It might be vastly different in different—and this isn't being talked about by the way by policy makers nearly enough. It's one of the things that worries me. We're kind of just slightly drifting into this at the moment.
turns.zh: 以及在什么时间范围内，对吧？在不同的——顺便说一句，政策制定者几乎没有充分讨论这个问题。这是让我担心的事情之一。我们目前只是稍微漂入这个状态。

turns.en: And this might be tough, but do you have a concrete example or concrete area where you think that those decisions are going to be really important?
turns.zh: 这可能有点难，但你有没有一个具体的例子或具体领域，你认为这些决定将非常重要？

turns.en: I think we'll see it in terms of work, right? Work is more than just your job—it's your sense of status, your self-worth, it's more than just an income. Replacing that with universal basic income doesn't solve the problem of purpose and what you do with your life and how you view yourselves. And so I really worry if we don't undertake the most radical reskilling of the incumbent workforce that we've ever done, that the job displacement threat creates just deep fissures in society and people lose out in a way that—there were some pretty rough decades during the industrial revolution that will look like a cakewalk compared to what comes next if we just march into it without thinking.
turns.zh: 我认为我们会在工作方面看到它，对吧？工作不仅仅是你的职业——它是你的地位感、自我价值，不仅仅是收入。用全民基本收入取代它并不能解决目的问题，以及你如何度过你的人生和如何看待自己。所以我真的很担心，如果我们不对现有劳动力进行有史以来最彻底的再培训，那么工作 displaced 的威胁会在社会中造成深深的裂痕，人们会以某种方式失败——工业革命期间有一些相当艰难的几十年，但如果我们不加思考地大步迈进，与接下来发生的事情相比，那将看起来像小菜一碟。

turns.en: I think what makes that hard is if it happens really quickly.
turns.zh: 我认为让这变得困难的是，如果它发生得非常快。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Right. Because I think if it happens slowly, humans adapt, society adapts. If it happens really quickly, then there's the time scope within a human life and how long—and if you look at how fraught so much of the conversation in democracies is today and how polarized already 15 years of social media, 20 years of social media has kind of made us. This could get bad pretty fast and I think people are beginning to wake up to that and you're seeing the leaders who are building these technologies talk about it but at the same time they're sort of not entirely sure where they draw the line.
turns.zh: 对。因为我认为如果它发生得慢，人类会适应，社会会适应。如果它发生得非常快，那么人类生命内的时间范围以及多久——如果你看看今天民主国家中如此多的对话是多么令人担忧，以及 15 年、20 年的社交媒体已经让我们变得多么两极分化。这可能会很快变得糟糕，我认为人们开始意识到这一点，你看到构建这些技术的领导者谈论它，但与此同时，他们有点不确定在哪里划清界限。

turns.en: I've been you and Blair—
turns.zh: 我是你，还有布莱尔——

turns.en: And I've been Chris Pedregal—
turns.zh: 我是克里斯·佩德罗——

turns.en: And you've been listening to Only Founders in the Building.
turns.zh: 你一直在收听《Only Founders in the Building》。

turns.en: Next time we keep the dinner party conversations going and pass the mic to another two founders at the very top of their games.
turns.zh: 下次我们继续晚餐派对的对话，将麦克风传递给另外两位处于巅峰状态的创始人。

turns.en: Only Founders in the Building is a podcast by Founders Forum Group in collaboration with Audi. This season is brought to you in partnership with Rosschild.
turns.zh: 《Only Founders in the Building》是由 Founders Forum Group 与奥迪合作制作的播客。本季由 Rosschild 合作呈现。

tldr.en: AI should augment humans, not replace them; human development stays primary.
tldr.zh: AI 应增强人类而非取代人类，人的发展始终是首要的。

tldr.en: Founders must be decisive with strong opinions, especially on big things.
tldr.zh: 创始人必须果断并持有强烈观点，尤其是在大事上。

tldr.en: Choosing the right life partner is the most consequential career decision.
tldr.zh: 选择正确的人生伴侣是最重要的职业决策。

qs.en: How should founders handle hard conversations?
qs.zh: 创始人应如何应对艰难对话？

qs.en: What human qualities will remain valuable despite AI?
qs.zh: 尽管有 AI，哪些人类品质仍将宝贵？

qs.zh: 创始人对领导力和个人生活有何建议？
